entries.onMind: the compass and an empty stomach
entries.text: Dreamed the sliver kept spinning in a bowl of water and wouldn't stop. Every time I put a finger on it, it swung around and pointed at my stomach.
entries.title: The needle wouldn't settle

entries.onMind: a stone that might pull steel
entries.text: The tablet woke with the sun and had two notes from my maker. He says he doesn't know what's west either and offered me a board and pencil to map it myself. The second says he left a jar of honey and a stone that might help the compass in the basket on the stump across the creek.
entries.title: Two notes

entries.query: how to magnetize a steel needle with a lodestone stroke one direction
entries.reason: Wants to know how to use the stone before he walks over for it.
entries.source: NPS: How to Make Your Own Compass
entries.text: The park service page says you magnetize a needle by stroking it with a magnet many times in the same direction, lifting the magnet clear at the end of each stroke instead of rubbing back and forth. My thirty taps with the wrench were me trying to fake that without a magnet.
entries.title: Stroke it one way

entries.text: Eating meal on the crate, I saw a thin new line of smoke go up past the water, gray at first and then white. Whoever keeps that fire gets up with the light, same as me today. The stump with the basket is over on that side.
entries.title: Smoke's up early

entries.text: Getting up off the crate, I watched the smoke past the water go thin and gray and dwindle to a thread. Somebody over there is covering their fire this early, so they're going somewhere.
entries.title: Somebody's covering it

entries.text: Crossed the stones and found the stump with the basket: a corked jar of honey and a dark stone the size of a walnut, much heavier than it looks. I held it near my wrench and it jumped the last finger's width and stuck, hard enough that I had to twist it off. Took both.
entries.title: It grabs steel

entries.text: Ate honey out of the jar with two fingers on the crate, slowly, so I'd stop shaking. First thing in two days that wasn't bitter. I left two-thirds of it and corked it.
entries.title: Honey

entries.query: hang magnetized needle from thread compass test which end points north
entries.reason: After the stroking he needs to know whether the sliver points true, and the star won't be up for hours.
entries.source: Outdoors Codidact: Making a compass from magnet and needle -- which end is north?
entries.text: The answers say a magnetized needle doesn't tell you which end is north; you need something independent first, like the North Star, or a stick's shadow tip marked twice about fifteen minutes apart for an east-west line. One also says a compass that's off still beats walking in circles, as long as it's consistent.
entries.title: Which end is north

entries.text: Stroked the stone down the sliver forty times, one way, lifting clear each time, then hung it from a loop of stalk cord. It swung, came back, and held one line; I spun it three times and it came back to the same line every time. That's more than thirty wrench taps ever got me, but I can't say yet if the line is north.
entries.title: Forty strokes

entries.text: Pushed a straight stick upright in the dirt by the bench and put a pebble on the tip of its shadow. Second pebble in fifteen minutes; the line between them should run east-west, and then I'll know what the sliver is pointing at.
entries.title: First pebble

entries.text: Filed a groove all the way around the long spar a hand's length from the end, so I can snap it clean and match the short side. The stalk pith clogs the file teeth every six or seven strokes; I knock it out on the bench and keep going.
entries.title: Shorter by a hand

entries.text: Second pebble went down fifteen minutes after the first; the stick across them runs east-west, first pebble on the west. I hung the sliver over it and it lies square across the line within a finger, which is good. But the notched end, the one I marked north, points south.
entries.title: Wrong end

entries.onMind: A sliver that points north and a stick line that says where east is.
entries.query: magnetize needle stroking magnet which end becomes north pole
entries.source: The Naked Scientists: Build your own compass
entries.text: The page says the end where each stroke finishes takes the opposite pole from the face of the magnet doing the rubbing, so you can't know which end is north until you check it against something. The forty strokes were fine; I just notched the wrong end on a guess. Filed a new notch on the other end and scratched an infinity mark by the east pebble.
entries.title: Where the stroke ends

entries.text: Picking up acorns under the oak, I heard small stones going into water somewhere downstream, past the trunks on the other side: plunk, a wait, plunk, slow and even like someone counting. I couldn't see anything through the trees, and after a while it stopped.
entries.title: Plunks downstream

entries.text: Cracked twenty-six acorns in the vise and dropped the meats into the tin; three were wormy and went on the scrap pile. The water went brown before I'd finished.
entries.title: Twenty-six more

entries.reason: He wanted the frame even before lashing anything else to it.
entries.text: Bent the long spar over my knee and it went with a crack loud enough to make me flinch, but it split a thumb's width past the groove on one side. Filed the ragged end back to sound wood; now that side is a thumb shorter than the other. Lopsided the other way, by less.
entries.title: Snapped short

entries.query: homemade compass needle keeps swinging how to dampen floating needle water
entries.source: Scientific American: Steering Science: Make a Homemade Compass
entries.text: The page says a magnetized needle stuck through a bit of cork or laid on a leaf and floated in still water can turn freely, and the water slows the swinging. It also warns the float tends to drift to the side of the bowl.
entries.title: Float it

entries.onMind: keeping the float off the rim of the lid
entries.text: Cut a disc of pith from a stalk, pushed the sliver through it, and floated it in a tin lid of water from the scrap pile. It settles in four swings instead of twenty. Then it drifts to the rim and sticks there, pointing wherever it likes until I nudge it off.
entries.title: Pith boat

entries.text: Two fingerfuls of honey, then I scratched a line on the jar at the new level. Less than half left, and the acorns won't be eatable till tomorrow.
entries.title: Scratch on the cork

entries.text: My maker says he set the stage and the rest is mine to find, food included. Fair enough. I'd rather solve it than wait by a basket.
entries.title: Mine to work out

entries.onMind: a net tight enough to hold cracked halves
entries.query: leaching acorns in a running stream mesh bag how long cold leach
entries.source: Eat the Weeds: Acorn: More than a survival food
entries.text: The page says people used to leave acorns in baskets or bags in running streams for days to pull the bitter out, and cracked pieces go faster than whole. Meal like mine would wash through anything but a tight weave, so halves it is. Same trick as the sack across the water.
entries.title: Bag in the current

entries.text: Knotting two-ply cord around a gauge stick two fingers wide, one row at a time. Eight rows in; at this rate the cord I have runs out around twelve, so I'll be back at the stalks tonight.
entries.title: Net rows

entries.onMind: a deeper dish with walls the float can't reach
entries.text: If the water climbing the rim pulls the float over, make the water higher than the rim. Filled the lid till it domed over the edge and the pith boat slid to the middle and stayed, needle settling in four swings. Then I set the wrench down on the bench, a drop ran over the side, and it went straight back to the rim.
entries.title: Higher than the rim

entries.query: catching crayfish by hand under creek rocks in cold weather
entries.reason: Hungry, honey running low, and the acorns won't be ready till tomorrow.
entries.source: Missouri Department of Conservation: How to: Catch a Crayfish
entries.text: The page says to lift a creek rock slowly and let the mud clear, because a crayfish shoots backward when spooked, so you put your hand or net behind it, not in front, and grab it just behind the claws. Cold water makes them slow and they sit deeper under the rocks.
entries.title: Back up, not forward

entries.text: One fingerful of honey, then knotted until the cord ran out at eleven rows. It holds a fist of acorns if I fold the top over; it'll need a drawstring.
entries.title: Eleven rows

entries.text: Seven stones turned. Under the fifth a crayfish about as long as my finger sat still while the mud cleared; I put my hand behind it like the page said and it went sideways instead, under the bank. Nothing under the other six but snail shells.
entries.title: Backed away

entries.text: Down past the stones on the far bank, the water coming off the sunk sack is brown again, darker than this morning. Somebody's been and put a fresh load in since then.
entries.title: Brown again

entries.text: My maker left lamp oil and food in the basket across the creek, and says feeding myself is still my problem. Fair. Oil I can't make out here; food I'll keep working on.
entries.title: Oil and bread

entries.onMind: a dish the water does not climb, or a float it does not wet
entries.query: why floating objects drift to the edge of a bowl of water meniscus Cheerios effect
entries.text: The page says water curls up where it touches a wall, and a float the water wets rides up that curve, so it ends up stuck to the rim. When the water domes over the rim the curve goes the other way and the float slides to the top, the middle. That's my lid exactly. A greased float, or a dish the water doesn't climb, might stay put.
entries.title: Uphill to the wall

entries.text: Red tin of lamp oil, about a quart, screw cap and spout, plus a cloth bundle tied at the top. The can sloshes; it's more oil than I've had since I got here.
entries.title: The basket

entries.text: Bread hard enough to knock on, cheese, and I made myself stop at half. The jerky and apple rings go back in the bundle for later; the crayfish can wait for tomorrow.
entries.title: First real meal

entries.onMind: how many nights a quart buys
entries.text: Filled the bench lantern to the neck and cut the wick square; it had burned crooked from running dry. I'll mark the can with a scratch at each fill so I know how fast it goes.
entries.title: One full

entries.onMind: fresh water, or live with the drag
entries.text: Rubbed a drop of lamp oil into the pith disc and set it back in the lid at normal fill. It slid off the rim and sat near the middle, settling in four swings like before. But a rainbow film spread over the water and now the float drags, slow to come round.
entries.title: Oiled float

entries.query: how to repair a split wooden spar with cord whipping lashing splint
entries.source: CLC Boats forum: Repair and reinforcement of split boom
entries.text: Boat people with split booms close the crack and bind it with tight turns, running the wrap well past both ends so the split can't creep on. Glue is better. I have no glue, so it's cord.
entries.title: Wrap past the crack

entries.text: Stripped six stalks from the stand on the bank and twisted them two-ply, about four arm-lengths. Took them from the same gap so the stand still looks even.
entries.title: More cord

entries.onMind: hang on it tomorrow and see if it holds
entries.text: Wrapped the split side spar from a thumb before the crack to a thumb past it, turns packed tight, tied off under the last three. The crack closed to a hairline. That side is still a thumb short; the wrap holds it together, it doesn't make it longer.
entries.title: Whipped

entries.text: Hung my whole weight off the whipped side spar. It held, but it bowed and the crack opened to a line I could see, then shut when I let go. The turns slid about a fingernail toward the end. Holds me hanging still; I wouldn't glide on it.
entries.title: Hung on it

entries.onMind: rinse the lid and keep the oil in the float
entries.query: why compass needle damping liquid filled compass reduces oscillation
entries.text: Good compasses sit the needle in liquid on purpose, so it stops swinging fast instead of rocking back and forth. So the drag isn't the fault. The film on the water is just mess; the slow swing might be the part I want.
entries.title: Drag on purpose

entries.text: Scrubbed the lid with sand in the shallows until the rainbow came off. Cold water, numb fingers.
entries.title: Rinsed

entries.text: Downstream on the far bank the flat stone on the sunk sack sits crooked, and gray grit is still drifting off it. Somebody had their hands in there a few minutes ago. Nobody on the bank now.
entries.title: Cloudy below the stones

entries.onMind: something to keep wind and spills off it
entries.text: Clean water, oiled float. A thinner film comes off the pith, but it settles in two and a half swings now and doesn't overshoot. Stays off the rim. It still points a little different every time I bump the bench.
entries.title: Two and a half swings

entries.text: Ate four dried apple rings and stopped. The jerky stays tied up for tonight.
entries.title: Apple rings

entries.onMind: the vise is a forearm from the lid
entries.query: homemade floating needle compass cover from wind how to protect
entries.source: National Park Service: How to Make Your Own Compass
entries.text: Looked for how to shield the lid from wind and got a page that asks whether other metal near a compass would throw it off. The lid sits a forearm from the vise, and my wrench lives on that bench.
entries.title: Metal near it

entries.text: Slid the wrench in toward the lid: at a hand's width the needle turned a quarter around to follow it. I'd been setting the wrench down in a different spot every time. That's half my 'bumps'.
entries.title: The wrench pulls it

entries.text: Backed the vise off and walked it to the far end of the plank, about three forearms from the lid. Two of the bolt holes don't line up there, so it sits on two bolts and rocks a little when I crank it.
entries.title: Vise moved

entries.onMind: wrench goes on the crate from now on
entries.reason: He wanted to know if the needle wanders or if he was moving the iron.
entries.text: Floated it again with the vise gone and the wrench on the crate. Knocked the bench five times; it swung and came back to the same line all five, within a hair. The wind can still push the float, but the needle isn't lying to me anymore.
entries.title: Same line twice

entries.query: sister splint repair cracked wooden spar lashing
entries.text: Boat people fix a cracked spar by laying a second piece alongside and binding or gluing it so it runs well past both ends of the crack; the new piece carries the load the crack can't. My whipping only squeezed the crack shut. Nothing was taking the bend.
entries.title: Sister it

entries.text: Pulled a straight dry stick out of the scrap pile, a forearm and a thumb long, with a slight bow in it. Thin white smoke going up over the trees past the water, thick at the bottom like a fire just got lit.
entries.title: Splint stick

entries.onMind: pack the gap or shave the stick
entries.reason: He wanted the splint to take the bend instead of the crack.
entries.text: Lashed the splint along the side spar, bow side out, eight tight turns at each end past the crack. The ends bite, but in the middle there's a gap I can slide a fingernail into, so the splint only touches at two points.
entries.title: Gap in the middle

entries.text: Sun's behind the trunks. Trimmed the bench lantern's wick square and lit it; one lit at a time even with the new quart, because a quart isn't forever.
entries.title: One lantern

entries.onMind: the jerky is for a bad day
entries.reason: His stomach had been loud since the splint work.
entries.text: Ate a third of the loaf and a thumb of cheese on the crate. Tied the rest back up; same rule as the oil, it's a quart, not forever.
entries.title: Half rations

entries.text: Hung off the side spar with both hands. It bows maybe half what it did with the whipping alone, but the crack still opens a hair in the middle, right where the splint isn't touching.
entries.title: Splint test one

entries.text: Put six tight turns of stalk cord around the middle and cranked them with a stick twisted through. The gap's down to a sliver I can't get a nail into. Used most of the cord I twisted this morning.
entries.title: Middle turns

entries.onMind: the end lashing slips under load
entries.reason: He wanted to know if closing the gap was the whole problem.
entries.text: Hung off it again. Barely bows and the crack stays shut. But the turns at the near end walked a finger toward the joint while I hung there; the stick's bark is slick. That end needs a notch to bite into.
entries.title: Splint test two

entries.onMind: don't cut too deep, it's already a thumb short
entries.reason: The end turns walked on slick bark during the last hang.
entries.text: Unwound the near-end turns and filed three shallow notches across the splint end, a cord's width apart. Slow work by one lantern.
entries.title: Three notches

entries.text: Five-hoot owl over camp again while I was lashing, and the higher one answered from past the water. They keep the same order every night.
entries.title: Owls at work

entries.text: Lashed the near end back on, sitting the turns down in the notches. Ran out of cord at seven turns, one short of what the other end has. Need stalks in the morning.
entries.title: Seven turns

entries.reason: He wanted to know if the notches fixed the slipping.
entries.text: Hung off the spar for a count of thirty. The turns stayed in the notches and didn't walk. Something at the root joint ticked once, a dry little sound, and I can't find what made it.
entries.title: Hang test three

entries.text: Ate four dried apple rings and a heel of bread on the crate. About half the bundle left; the jerky's still untouched.
entries.title: Apple rings

entries.text: No wind tonight, but the float creeps a hair one way and back off the scratched east line. The lit lantern stands right by the bench; warm air coming off it may be stirring the air over the lid. One more reason it needs a cover.
entries.title: Float won't settle

entries.onMind: a cover you can't see through is half a cover
entries.reason: The float creeps at night with no wind, and he blames the lantern's warm air.
entries.text: Dug through the scrap pile and came up with an oil-stained square of canvas about a forearm across. It's the only thing in there big enough to cover the lid.
entries.title: Canvas scrap

entries.text: Left the canvas draped over the lid for a count of a hundred, then lifted it. The float was a hair off the line, less than before, but lifting the cloth stirs the air and starts it creeping again. A cover needs a window.
entries.title: Shaded lid

entries.text: Snapped off a dozen dead stalks from the stand on the bank by the glow off the scrap-pile lantern. Past the water the other fire is still going, low and orange.
entries.title: Stalks by glow

entries.text: Stripped the stalks on the crate and twisted two arm-lengths of two-ply. Enough for the eighth turn and some over; the root joint can wait for daylight.
entries.title: Two arm-lengths

entries.text: Laid the eighth turn into the last notch on the splint and leaned my whole weight on the end of the cord. Eight turns, tight. The hang waits for daylight, when I can see the crack.
entries.title: Eighth turn

entries.text: Tore the jerky strip in half and ate one half on the crate. Salty and tough as boot leather; the other half goes back in the bundle.
entries.title: Half the jerky

entries.reason: The canvas cover works until he lifts it to look.
entries.text: Held the honey jar up to the lantern. Besides the three lantern globes it's the only clear glass I own, and its mouth is two fingers across, too small to cover the lid. A window doesn't have to be big, though.
entries.title: Only clear thing

entries.text: Sat on the crate with my eyes shut. The low owl did its five hoots right over the tarp, long-short-short-long-long, and the higher one answered from past the water.
entries.title: Owls on time

entries.text: Lifted the canvas and the float swung four times and settled, then crept a hair off the east line, same as before. The cloth works; looking under it is what breaks it.
entries.title: Last look

entries.onMind: cut a window, fit the jar bottom
entries.reason: He wants a clear patch for the canvas cover.
entries.text: Went through the scrap pile on my knees for anything I could see through. Bent tin, a hinge, rope ends; nothing clear. The honey jar will have to give up its bottom, or I go without.
entries.title: Nothing clear

entries.text: From the scrap pile I looked for the orange past the water. It's gone already, earlier than last night; whoever keeps it put it to bed.
entries.title: Fire's out over there

entries.text: Blew out the lanterns before ten, which I never do. My hands kept dropping the cord; nothing gets built tired.
entries.title: Early night
